ⓘ Where do I get the model?

Guardian Shield's AI detection is 100% on-device — the app has NO internet permission, so the model file can only come from you.

1) On this phone, open any browser and search: nsfw_mobilenet2 tflite — open-source content-filter models on GitHub or Hugging Face (usually 2–30 MB).

2) Download the .tflite file (it lands in Downloads).

3) Back here, tap Import and pick the file.

Guardian verifies the file really loads BEFORE it is installed — a broken download is rejected with a clear message, never silently. And after import, detection uses the new model right away — no app restart needed.

Everything else in Guardian Shield works with or without the model; AI detection simply stays off until you add one.

How Guardian Shield protects you — straight answers, no marketing.
How does the AI blocking work?

Guardian Shield reads on-screen content through the Accessibility service and checks it with an AI model (TensorFlow Lite) that runs entirely on your phone. Each check splits the screen into sections that vote; when harmful content scores above your adjustable threshold (default 0.72), the shield acts. No image or text ever leaves the device.
What are strikes and temp blocks?

The first and second AI detection of an app show a warning card. A third detection applies a temporary full block — 15, 30 or 60 minutes, your choice in Settings. Stay away for 10 minutes and the strike counter resets. Three full blocks within 2 hours escalate to a 24-hour day block, and after any block expires a 3-minute grace period passes before AI blocking resumes.
What are “Not Sensitive” reports and the cooling-off queue?

Telling the app a detection was wrong fixes low-confidence mistakes immediately. But when the AI was highly confident (0.82 or more), your report joins a deliberate delay queue instead of applying instantly — 2h for the first recent report, then 4h, 8h, 16h, up to 24h. Settings → Pending Reports shows everything queued and lets you cancel before it applies. The delay is the feature: it keeps a craving from silently retraining the shield.

Time-Lock locks your settings for a period you choose. While it’s active, settings can’t be edited, the dashboard toggle is frozen, and uninstall protection is at its strictest. Turn it on while you’re motivated, so a future weak moment can’t quietly switch the shield off.
I forgot my PIN. What now?

Two recovery paths, both deliberately slow: (1) the recovery code you wrote down at PIN setup — enter it on the PIN Recovery screen (5 tries, then a 30-minute wait); (2) a timed reset — request it, wait 48 hours, then set a new PIN. Neither path wipes your rules or history, and there is no instant reset — that’s the point.
What does the accountability partner do?

Add a trusted person’s name and email in Settings → Accountability. When protection is paused, a tamper attempt is logged, or a high-confidence report is queued, you get a notification with Email and Share actions. Tapping opens your mail app or share sheet pre-addressed and pre-written — the final send is always yours. Nothing is sent silently; the app has no server and no automatic sending.
Backups — what’s included, what never is?

Settings → Backup writes one JSON file, kept by you: app rules, keywords, schedules, settings and your partner contact. It never contains block history, your PIN, the recovery code or any Time-Lock state. After a reinstall, Restore from that file to bring your setup back.

Yes. Detection runs fully on-device, and the app doesn’t even declare the internet permission — it physically cannot send your screen content or history anywhere. Tamper and crash logs are stored locally on the phone for you to read or share yourself. (An optional Firebase Crashlytics hook exists in the source, but it only activates in a build where the developer adds their own google-services.json — the public release build has none.)
Can protection be bypassed? The honest answer.

Yes, partly — and we won’t pretend otherwise. Safe Mode, a force-stop from system Settings, or a computer with USB debugging can weaken or remove protection; no app on unrooted Android can fully prevent those. What Guardian Shield does: bounce the risky Settings screens whenever the service is alive, detect and log tampering, re-request Device Admin the moment a revocation is noticed, and alert you (and your partner, if set). The design goal is friction plus visibility — not an unbreakable cage.

Android needs your explicit OK before any app may dismiss another app’s notifications. On the next screen, switch on Guardian Shield.\n\nWhat this lets the shield do: cancel shade previews from apps you’ve blocked (list, schedule or AI temp block), and — when your keyword filter is on — hide notifications whose visible text matches your keywords. Everything is processed on-device; the app has no internet permission, so nothing can be uploaded. Revoke any time in the same system screen. A preview can still flash for a split second before it’s cancelled — no app can avoid that on unrooted Android.
Do blocked apps still show notification previews?

By default, yes — Android posts a blocked app’s notifications to the shade, preview included. Turn on Settings → Notification shade shield and grant “Notification access”: previews from blocked apps (list, schedule or temp block) are then cancelled, and with your keyword filter on, any notification whose visible text matches your keywords is hidden too. One honest limit: a preview can flash for a split second before cancellation — unrooted Android gives no way to prevent that.
